title: A Missing License Plate Caught the Oklahoma City Bomber
central_question: How was the Oklahoma City bomber already in a jail cell before the FBI knew his name?
content_notes: Closed case: McVeigh was convicted on 2 Jun 1997 and executed on 11 Jun 2001; Terry Nichols was also convicted. 168 people were killed, including 19 children: the explosion, the building, the victims, rescue scenes and injuries are never depicted, and no famous photograph is recreated. McVeigh appears only as an anonymous rim-lit silhouette (not a likeness, never his booking photo), is never posed heroically, and none of his statements or beliefs are quoted. The trooper is a generic figure and is not named. No weapon is shown. The car is a generic 1970s yellow sedan; the rental counter carries no brand name, colours or logo; the jail, highway and lab are generic. The axle's number is never shown (masked). No real photograph, police or court material, sketch or document is imitated: every card is our own typed graphic, and the composite sketch is shown only from the back of the pad. No dialogue is invented. Legal status verified 2026-10-12.

lines.text: The Oklahoma City bomber was in a jail cell before the FBI knew his name.
Because of a missing license plate.
His truck bomb killed 168 people, including 19 children.
Within about 90 minutes a trooper stopped a car with no license plate.
He was jailed on gun and traffic charges.
Meanwhile a truck axle's vehicle identification number led the FBI to Kansas.
Sketches from a rental shop there led to a name: Timothy McVeigh.
Agents ran the name. He was already in jail,
A missing license plate held him.

claims.text: Timothy McVeigh was already in custody, after a traffic stop for a missing license plate on the morning of the bombing, when the FBI identified him by name on 20-21 April 1995.
The truck bomb that exploded outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City at 9:02 a.m. on 19 April 1995 killed 168 people, including 19 children.

Within about 90 minutes of the bombing (FBI: 'just 90 minutes'; the published 10:20 a.m. stop time makes it about 78), an Oklahoma Highway Patrol trooper stopped a pale yellow 1977 Mercury Marquis with no rear license plate on I-35 in Noble County, north of Oklahoma City.

The trooper found a concealed handgun; the driver was arrested on misdemeanor weapons and traffic/vehicle charges and booked into the Noble County Jail in Perry, Oklahoma. (No weapon is shown on screen.)
The rental truck's rear axle housing, recovered from the wreckage, carried (part of) its vehicle identification number.
The number was traced to a truck rented on 17 April 1995 from Elliott's Body Shop, a truck-rental agent in Junction City, Kansas (the rental company is not named on screen).
Shop staff helped the FBI make composite sketches; at a Junction City motel the sketch was matched to a guest registered as Tim McVeigh, which gave agents a name.

A records check showed Timothy McVeigh was still in custody in the Noble County Jail; on 21 April the FBI asked for him to be held, shortly before he was due to be released (History.com, The Globe and Mail; the FBI says the hold kept him from being released).
A federal jury found McVeigh guilty on all 11 counts on 2 June 1997; he was sentenced to death and executed by lethal injection on 11 June 2001, the first federal execution since 1963.
Terry Nichols was convicted on federal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges in December 1997 (life sentence) and on 161 state murder counts in 2004. On screen only.
FUN FACT (card only): the Mercury Marquis McVeigh was driving when he was arrested joined the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum's collection in 2013 and is displayed there.
